source.title: Preference Instability in Reward Models: Detection and Mitigation via Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Shun-Chang Liu; Xin Chen; Belen Martin-Urcelay; Francesco Croce

record.tranche_reason: The study compares SAE-encoded features with raw hidden-state features to test whether a sparse dictionary can recover information about preference-inverting perturbations in reward models. This bears on V4, but is not a test of the original toy-model superposition method.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the reported detection comparisons and the described feature-shift analysis. Mitigation accuracy results are not included: they assess mitigation strategies rather than directly testing whether SAEs recover sparse features. Results cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained-style Gated SAEs as a tool to detect and mitigate preference-inverting perturbations in reward models. Its results are its own method's performance: an SAE-feature MLP versus raw, PCA or linear-probe detectors, and SAE versus raw steering. It does not measure whether the reward models contain sparse features an SAE recovers (reconstruction, interpretability, feature quality). It also does not measure feature spread across neurons, capacity, geometry or feature dimensionality. Superposition (Elhage et al., 2022) is cited only as motivation for why dense hidden states are entangled.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that reward-model preference instability stems from over-reliance on unstable features. They report that SAEs expose a separable pattern in sparse latent space that enables detection and retraining-free mitigation. They make no claim about SAE features being complete or canonical units, nor about superposition itself.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains Gated SAEs on reward-model activations and compares classifiers on SAE versus raw features; it does not use the original toy-network superposition setup or its geometric measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Detection and mitigation vary with perturbation type, dataset, and layer. The paper also evaluates transfer to unseen injection templates and paraphrases from a different rewriter; detection retains an SAE advantage, while unseen-rewriter paraphrase mitigation is harder.

fits_no_version.finding: Classifiers on 16k-dim Gated SAE latents detect preference-inverting perturbations far better than identical MLPs on raw states. They also beat linear probes and PCA bases (e.g. paraphrase on HH: 92.7 vs 51.4 accuracy). Perturbation shifts also concentrate in fewer SAE dimensions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latent bases make perturbation-related signal more separable for downstream detection and steering than dense hidden-state bases.

record.problems: Results concern preference-inversion detection in reward models on selected perturbation families and datasets; generality to other LLM features is not established. Reported detection comparisons provide no uncertainty estimates. Figure 2 is described qualitatively in the text, with plotted values only.
record.rows_left_out: Mitigation results in Tables 3, 7, and 10 and Figure 3 are omitted because their reported outcomes concern correction performance, not direct measurement of SAE feature recovery. Table 9 repeats the main detection comparison for Poisoned-Reward-7B on Anthropic HH while adding detector baselines; those duplicate main results are not separately rowed.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All: no capacity or polysemanticity analysis.
No measurement of feature spread across neurons, SAE reconstruction, or interpretability of recovered features. The SAE is used only as a detection and steering basis.
All: no completeness, stability or canonicity tests.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'supports' labels are removed. Better downstream classification on an SAE basis is an application result, not a test of whether the model stores sparse superposed features. The SAE basis also has a much larger input dimension than raw states (16384 vs d), so the comparison does not isolate feature recovery. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometric structure.
Whether polysemanticity results from competition for limited representational capacity.
Whether polysemanticity can arise without capacity pressure.

The study tests SAE recovery of perturbation-related information in reward models, not feature spread across neurons. It does not establish that the findings generalize to LLM representations broadly or to features beyond those related to the tested perturbations.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model's representation.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Skywork-Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Compare the fraction of feature dimensions above a normalized pairwise-difference shift threshold in SAE features and raw hidden states.
rows.measure: Fraction of feature dimensions whose normalized pairwise-difference shift exceeds threshold ε
rows.note: The text says SAE curves have more near-zero-shift dimensions at low thresholds and more mass at high thresholds, indicating concentrated strongly shifted dimensions.
rows.check: Distribution of perturbation-induced shifts across SAE vs raw dimensions. This is a separability property for the detection task, not evidence that the model's features are sparse or superposed. Layer is presumably 12 but not stated for the figure.
